ai.title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
ai.brief: The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real. Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions” into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign.

sec.title: FORGE Lab uses agentic tools to identify memory safety issues in Rust
sec.brief: In this article How we found and validated the bugs Pattern 1: Trusting code not to panic Pattern 2: Trusting user-provided implementations to be correct Pattern 3: Trusting the underlying system Why Rust still matters and advancing vulnerability discovery with AI Rust's high bar is hard to meet but worth keeping Microsoft’s FORGE Lab found several memory safety issues in Rust’s standard library (std and core), including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The research used Hyenas, FORGE’s frontier research version of codename MDASH, an AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system. The findings reveal three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system. Rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting.
